sections.h: SSH: log in to another machine with keys
sections.body:
SSH (Secure Shell) gives you a shell on another machine over an encrypted connection. Running `ssh ubuntu@192.168.64.5` logs you in as ubuntu. Passwords work, but keys are safer and quicker. A key pair is two files:

- The private key, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, stays on your laptop. It works like a password, so never copy it anywhere else.
- The public key, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`, is safe to share. You put it on servers and in GitHub.

Create a pair with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"`, and set a passphrase when it asks. Afterwards, `ls -l ~/.ssh` shows the private key with mode `-rw-------` (600) and the public one with `-rw-r--r--` (644).

A server keeps the public keys it trusts in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, one per line. When you connect, it checks that you hold the matching private key. The private key itself never leaves your laptop.

Trust also runs the other way. The first time you connect, ssh shows the server's fingerprint and asks `Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])?`. Saying yes stores it in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. If that fingerprint ever changes, ssh refuses to connect, because someone may be pretending to be your server.

Four more tools make SSH pleasant:

- The file `~/.ssh/config` gives hosts short names, so `ssh devbox` replaces a long command (see the files below).
- The ssh-agent program holds your unlocked key, so you type the passphrase once. On a Mac, `ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519` keeps it in your Keychain.
- `scp app.log devbox:/tmp/` copies a file over SSH.
- `rsync -av logs/ devbox:/tmp/logs/` copies a folder. Run it again and it sends only what changed.

sections.h: Your first bash script
sections.body:
A script is a text file of commands. Three things make it runnable:

1. The first line is a shebang, `#!/usr/bin/env bash`. It tells the system to run the file with bash, wherever bash is installed. Use it on your Mac too, so scripts behave the same everywhere.
2. The file needs the execute bit: `chmod +x script.sh` (Day 6).
3. You run it with a path, `./script.sh`, because your current folder is not in PATH.

Scripts get their arguments as numbered variables:

- `$1`, `$2` and so on are the arguments, and `$0` is the script's own name.
- `$#` is how many arguments there are.
- `"$@"` is all of them, each kept as a separate word. Running `./args.sh deploy "eu west" 3` gives three arguments, and `eu west` stays one of them.

Quoting decides what the shell does to a value. It causes more script bugs than anything else:

- Single quotes keep everything literal: `echo 'Hello, $name'` prints `Hello, $name`.
- Double quotes still replace variables: `echo "Hello, $name"` prints `Hello, Ada Lovelace`.
- No quotes means the shell splits the value on spaces and expands globs in it. With `file="my notes.txt"`, `ls $file` looks for two files, while `ls "$file"` works.

So write `"$var"` and `"$(command)"` in double quotes unless you have a reason not to.

Every command returns an exit code, and so does your script. The variable `$?` holds the last one. `exit 0` ends a script with success, and `exit 1` (or any number up to 255) with failure. CI systems such as GitHub Actions (Day 18) look only at that number: anything but 0 fails the step.

sections.h: Conditions, loops and functions
sections.body:
The `if` keyword runs a command and checks its exit code. In bash, `[[ ... ]]` is a command made for tests:

- `[[ -f app.log ]]` is true if the file exists, and `-d` checks for a directory.
- `[[ "$a" == "$b" ]]` compares strings, and `[[ $n -gt 9 ]]` compares numbers. Its friends are `-lt`, `-ge`, `-le`, `-eq` and `-ne`.
- `if grep -q ERROR app.log; then ... fi` works because grep returns 0 on a match.
- The older `[ ... ]`, also called `test`, works in every shell but has more quoting traps. Prefer `[[ ]]` in bash.

Loops repeat work:

- `for f in logs/*.log; do echo "$f: $(grep -c ERROR "$f")"; done` prints an error count for each file.
- `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < app.log` reads a file line by line, keeping spaces and backslashes exactly as they are.

A function is a named group of commands, such as `log() { echo "healthcheck: $*" >&2; }`. Inside it, `$1` and friends are the function's own arguments, and `local` keeps a variable from leaking out. The line `return 1` sets the function's exit code, which `if` and `||` can test. And `>&2` sends a message to stderr, so it never mixes with the script's real output.

sections.h: Safe scripts: strict mode, trap and ShellCheck
sections.body:
By default bash forgives too much. A failed command does not stop the script, a typo in a variable name becomes an empty string, and a pipe hides failures. One line at the top fixes most of that: `set -euo pipefail`.

- `-e` exits as soon as a command fails. Commands in an `if` test or before `&&` and `||` are exempt, because there a failure is expected.
- `-u` makes an unset variable an error. Under it, `echo "deploying to $DEPLOY_DIR"` stops with `DEPLOY_DIR: unbound variable` instead of deploying to an empty path.
- `-o pipefail` makes a pipe fail when any part fails. `cat nope.txt | sort` exits 0 without it and 1 with it.

Strict mode has a cost. Because grep exits 1 when it finds nothing, under `-e` an empty search ends your script. Write `grep -q FATAL app.log || true` when no match is fine. For a variable that must be set, `${DIR:?DIR is not set}` stops the script with that message. Here is why that matters: with an empty `DIR`, the line `rm -rf "$DIR/"*` expands to every folder under `/`.

To clean up whatever happens, use `trap 'cleanup commands' EXIT`. It runs when the script ends, on success or failure, so temp files made with `mktemp` always get deleted.

Finally, run ShellCheck on every script: `shellcheck script.sh`. It is installed in the lab container, and on a Mac you add it with `brew install shellcheck`. It knows hundreds of bash traps and explains each one with a code. For an unquoted variable it reports SC2086, "Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting." ShellCheck exits non-zero when it finds problems, so CI can run it too. Once a script needs real data structures or grows past about a hundred lines, write it in Python or Kotlin instead.

code.title: healthcheck.sh
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# healthcheck.sh: check that hello-devops is alive and ready.
# Usage:    ./healthcheck.sh [BASE_URL]     (default: http://localhost:8000)
# Settings: RETRIES (default 5) and DELAY in seconds (default 2).
# Exit code: 0 healthy, 1 a check failed, 2 wrong usage. CI reads this number.
set -euo pipefail

if [[ $# -gt 1 ]]; then
  echo "usage: $0 [BASE_URL]" >&2
  exit 2
fi

base_url="${1:-http://localhost:8000}"
retries="${RETRIES:-5}"
delay="${DELAY:-2}"

# log: print a message to stderr, so it never mixes with real output.
log() {
  echo "healthcheck: $*" >&2
}

# check PATH: ask for one URL until it answers 200, or give up.
check() {
  local path="$1"
  local attempt code
  for ((attempt = 1; attempt <= retries; attempt++)); do
    # -s: no progress bar. -o /dev/null: throw the body away.
    # -w '%{http_code}': print only the status code (000 if nothing answered).
    # --max-time 5: give up on this try after 5 seconds.
    # || true: curl fails when it cannot connect; we handle that ourselves.
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 5 "${base_url}${path}" || true)
    if [[ "$code" == "200" ]]; then
      log "OK   ${path} answered 200"
      return 0
    fi
    log "try ${attempt}/${retries}: ${path} answered ${code}"
    if ((attempt < retries)); then
      sleep "$delay"
    fi
  done
  log "FAIL ${path} never answered 200"
  return 1
}

check /healthz || exit 1
check /readyz || exit 1
log "all checks passed for ${base_url}"

interview.q: What does `set -euo pipefail` do, and what is the catch?
interview.a: It makes bash stop on the first failing command (-e), treat unset variables as errors (-u) and fail a pipeline when any part fails (-o pipefail). Together they stop a script from carrying on after a failure and reporting success. The catch is that some commands use non-zero codes for normal results. For example, grep returns 1 for no match, so you add `|| true` where that is fine. Also, `-e` has exceptions inside conditions, so treat it as a safety net and still check the important steps yourself.

interview.q: How does SSH key authentication work?
interview.a: You generate a key pair; the private key stays on your machine and the public key goes into the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. When you connect, the server sends a challenge that only the holder of the private key can sign. It checks the signature with the public key, so the private key never crosses the network. The client also checks the server's host key against `known_hosts`, which protects you from talking to an impostor.

interview.q: Why can't a script change the environment variables of the terminal that ran it?
interview.a: Running `./script.sh` starts a new bash process, a child of your shell. The child gets a copy of the parent's environment, and an export in the child changes only that copy, which disappears when the child exits. To change your current shell you `source` the file, which runs its lines in the current process. The same rule is why `cd` inside a script does not move your terminal.

deeper.body:
Three details make the difference between a script that works on your laptop and one that works everywhere.

First, the Mac's own bash is old. macOS still ships bash 3.2 from 2007, and its default shell has been zsh since 2019. A script with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` runs under that bash 3.2 unless you installed a newer one with Homebrew. Linux servers and CI runners have bash 5. So avoid bash 4 features in scripts you share, such as associative arrays (`declare -A`) and `mapfile`. Everything in `healthcheck.sh` works in both versions.

Second, strict mode is a trade-off, and some experienced engineers argue against `set -e` ([one such argument](https://jmmv.dev/2018/03/shell-readability-strict-mode.html)). Its exceptions are subtle. It does not fire inside `if` tests, on the left of `&&` or `||`, or inside a function called from such a place. A script can therefore keep running after a failure you expected to stop it. The practical answer most teams use is to keep strict mode as a safety net and still check the steps that matter explicitly, as `healthcheck.sh` does with `check /healthz || exit 1`.

Third, when a script misbehaves, make it show its work. Run it with `bash -x script.sh`, or put `set -x` near the top. bash then prints every command after expansion, with a `+` in front, before running it. You see the real values of variables and the real result of each glob, which is Day 3's `echo` habit, built in. Turn it off again with `set +x`.

A last habit for scripts that run in CI: send messages for humans to stderr and keep stdout for data. `healthcheck.sh` does this with its `log` function. Then `./healthcheck.sh 2> /dev/null` stays quiet, and a later step can still pipe the real output into jq or grep without the chatter getting in the way.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between an absolute and a relative path?
flashcards.back: An absolute path starts at `/` and works from anywhere; a relative path starts from the current folder.

flashcards.front: How do you preview what a glob will match?
flashcards.back: Put `echo` in front of the command, as in `echo rm *.log`.

flashcards.front: Which grep options ignore case, count, number lines and invert the match?

flashcards.back: Without `-E`, `|` is a plain character. Use `grep -E 'WARN|ERROR'`.

flashcards.front: In a regular expression, what do `.` and `*` mean?
flashcards.back: `.` is any one character; `*` is zero or more of the item before it.
Files named *.log that were last changed more than 7 days ago.
It sends both normal output and error messages to out.txt.
uniq only merges duplicate lines that are next to each other.

flashcards.front: What do the modes 755, 644 and 600 mean?
flashcards.back: rwxr-xr-x, rw-r--r-- and rw-------: owner, group and others, with r=4, w=2, x=1.

flashcards.front: What do exit codes 130, 143 and 137 mean?
flashcards.back: The process ended from Ctrl+C (SIGINT), SIGTERM or SIGKILL: 128 plus the signal number.

flashcards.front: What does `docker stop` send to a container?
flashcards.back: SIGTERM first, then SIGKILL if it is still running after 10 seconds.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `systemctl enable` and `systemctl start`?
flashcards.back: enable makes it start at boot, start runs it now, and `enable --now` does both.

flashcards.front: Can a child process change its parent's environment variables?
flashcards.back: No. It gets a copy, and its changes never flow back.

flashcards.front: Where does your SSH public key go on a server?
flashcards.back: Into `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` of the user you log in as.

quiz.q: You are in `/work/logs/archive`. Which path reaches `/work/app.log`?
quiz.why: One `..` climbs to `/work/logs` and the second to `/work`, where app.log lives.

quiz.q: Which command lists the files under `server` that are larger than 1 MB?
quiz.why: find tests every file under a folder, and `-size +1M` keeps those over 1 MB.

quiz.q: `grep -c 200 app.log` prints 16, but `grep -c -w 200 app.log` prints 14. Why the difference?
options: `-w` skips the first and last lines
Two lines contain 200 inside a longer word
quiz.why: `1200ms` and `2001` contain 200, and `-w` only matches 200 standing alone as a word.

quiz.q: Which pipeline counts requests per status code (field 9), most common first?
quiz.why: Sort first so uniq can count neighbours, then sort the counts as numbers in reverse.

quiz.q: What does `2> /dev/null` do at the end of a command?
options: Saves errors into a file called null
Stops the command on its first error
quiz.why: It points stderr (2) at /dev/null, which discards everything written to it.

quiz.q: `kill 4242` did not stop a process, even after a minute. What is the usual next step?
quiz.why: The process is ignoring SIGTERM, so SIGKILL (9), which cannot be caught, is the last resort.

quiz.q: `ls -ld reports` shows `drwxr-x---`, owned by `app:ops`. User sam is not in ops. What can sam do?
options: Nothing: no listing and no entry
List the names but not enter it
Enter it and read files by name
quiz.why: The others triplet is `---`, so sam has no read, write or execute rights on the folder.

quiz.q: A deploy script runs `./build.sh | tee build.log` and then deploys. It deploys even when the build fails. Which line at the top stops it?
quiz.why: With pipefail the pipe fails when build.sh fails, and -e then stops the script.

quiz.q: A team made 40 deployments last month, and 6 of them needed a hotfix or a rollback. Which DORA metric is 15 percent?
quiz.why: Change fail rate is the share of deployments that needed immediate action: 6 of 40 is 15 percent.

quiz.q: You installed tree inside `docker run -it --rm ubuntu:24.04 bash`, typed exit, and ran the same command again. Why is tree missing now?
options: tree only works on a Mac
apt needs sudo inside a container
`--rm` deleted the container; each run starts clean
quiz.why: Each run makes a new container from the unchanged image, and `--rm` removed the old one with its changes.
